draft.title: Managing your superannuation
card: Funds charge fees, which are taken out of your balance. Compare fees and returns between funds, because high fees can eat into your savings over many years.
People who change jobs can end up with several super accounts. Each may charge fees, so combining them into one can cut the total fees paid.
Super can become lost when a fund cannot reach its member, for example after a move. The Australian Taxation Office (ATO) can help people find lost super.
Checking your super now and then helps you keep more of it for retirement.
draft.remember: Check fees and returns, combine accounts and find lost super to keep more savings.

a.q: Why can holding three super accounts cost a worker more than holding one?
opts: Each account may charge its own fees
Each account earns a lower return by law
The government taxes every extra account
Only the first account can receive employer payments
a.why: Each fund can charge fees, so several accounts mean several sets of fees taken from the savings. The other options are not true: extra accounts are not taxed for being extra, and they do not earn lower returns by law.
a.clue: Think about what each fund takes out of the balance.

b.q: Priya, 24, worked at a café, then a shop, then an office, and now has three super accounts. She thinks one may be lost. What should she do?
opts: Ask the ATO to find any lost super, then combine accounts
Leave the accounts alone, as fees stop when she changes jobs
Close the accounts and spend the money to avoid fees
Pick the fund with the highest fees, as it must be the best
b.why: The ATO can help people find lost super, and combining accounts can cut the fees paid. Leaving the accounts alone is tempting, but fees can keep being taken from each one after she changes jobs.
b.clue: Who can help find lost super, and how can fees be cut?

a.best: Each account may charge its own fees

b.best: Ask the ATO to find any lost super, then combine accounts
